Background

It’s not just semantics
• Nitpicking over the meaning of words may seem trivial, but for
complicated topics, it’s essential to understand exactly what
we’re talking about.
• In education, terminology carries weight because it shapes how we
think, communicate, and make decisions.
• Misunderstandings or differing interpretations of key terms can lead
to misaligned policies, ineffective practices, or even public mistrust in
the system.
• For example, what do we mean by “assessment”? Is it a test, a
portfolio, an observation? How we define it determines how we
design it and what we expect from it.

It’s not just semantics
• Over the last decade (and even further), the term "assessment" has
expanded far beyond its traditional scope—a shift many of you have
likely observed.
• Historically, "assessment" primarily referred to standardized testing,
often used for accountability purposes or to evaluate large-scale trends
in student achievement.
• The term, however, encompasses a wide range of tools and practices:
formative assessments, performance tasks, classroom checks for
understanding, adaptive assessments, through-course assessments, and
even measures of non-academic skills like social-emotional learning.
• I embrace this broader application of the term "assessment" as it reflects
the reality of the diverse ways we assess in education.

So what’s the big deal?
• Assessments, I would argue, regardless of what type, are point in
time exercises in data collection.
• The term assessment data often connotes something quantitative,
derived through standardized procedures.
• However, assessment data can encompass qualitative data as well.
• As many of you are aware, current assessments often promise
much more than just reporting data on what student know and
can do.
• Current assessments often claim to inform instruction.

Assessment & Learning
• The term assessment has been and is currently used in some ways unfamiliar
(and wrong) to me. A case in point:
• The terms Assessment and Learning are appearing more frequently together:
Assessment of Learning, Assessments to measure student learning.
• Learning is an unobserved process that happens over time whereas an
assessment indicates what a student knows and can do at a given point in
time.
• We infer that learning has occurred by changes in what a student knows and
can do (which is what assessments, at their best, tell us). I do not think that
assessments measure learning.
• We make inferences about learning based upon observations (i.e.,
assessments, plural) over time.

One last peeve
• If I had a dollar for every time I’ve heard:
“That assessment wasn’t designed for that
purpose and therefore can’t be used that way.”

• It’s the quick and easy way for “experts” to shut down the use of an assessment that they
find questionable.
• Yes, design is important, however, life is filled with examples of tools originally designed for
one purpose being “validated” for others (my wife uses a screw driver to open tight jar lids)
• And note, tools designed for a purpose don’t always work for that purpose (who
remembers Clippy?).
• That said, assessment use absolutely does need to be validated (regardless if it was
designed or not designed for that purpose).

Innovation in Assessment
• Assessments have evolved significantly in the last two decades:
• Modality: Transition from traditional paper-and-pencil tests to online platforms,
enabling greater efficiency, flexibility, and accessibility.
• Adaptivity: Emergence of adaptive testing, where items are dynamically adjusted
based on student responses, providing more precise measures of ability.
• Automated Scoring: Advances in technology have enabled automated scoring for
written responses, offering faster feedback and reducing human scoring biases.
• Complex Item Types: Incorporation of interactive and multimedia-rich items that
assess higher-order skills and mirror real-world problem-solving.
• Intererim & Through-Course Assessment: Introduction of modular assessment
designs that evaluate student progress throughout the course, rather than relying
solely on end-of-course exams.

Accountability & Assessment
• Due to the way in which NCLB inextricably linked assessment
results and accountability, the two are often conflated.
• Dislike of accountability systems often overlaps with dislike of
the assessments that provide the data for the accountability
systems.
• Innovations in large scale assessment, particularly over the
last decade, have been in large part driven by frustration
associated with their (ab)use in accountability systems.

What’s the problem?
• Criticisms of current large scale assessments include:
• Delayed feedback: Results aren’t timely to impact
instruction.
• Lack of instructional utility: Results aren’t instructionally
useful.
• Unintended consequences: Teaching to the test,
narrowing/altering the scope and sequence of the
curriculum. High stakes and stress.

What’s the problem?
• Is the problem the assessment or the way in which the
assessment is used (or both in some measure).
• The likely answer is both.
• I’m of the opinion that the much bigger issue is the way in
which the data derived from the assessments is used.
• Accountability being the driving force for how data gets
used is largely to blame for this.
• I’m skeptical that the “right” assessment will correct the
woes associated with inadequate or faulty data use.

Example: Through Course Assessment (TCA)
• One of the latest ideas to improve large scale education
assessment is with through course assessment designs.
• Through-course assessment refers to a system where
students complete multiple assessments spaced throughout
the academic year, as opposed to a single, end-of-year
summative test.
• These assessments are designed to collectively measure the
same standards and competencies typically addressed by a
traditional summative assessment.

Implications for Accountability Systems

What’s the problem?
• Criticisms of current large scale assessments include:
• Delayed feedback: Results aren’t timely to impact interventions
and instruction.
• Lack of instructional utility: Results aren’t instructionally useful
due to curricular (mis)alignment, grain size of results, etc.
• Unintended consequences: Teaching to the test, narrowing/
altering the scope and sequence of the curriculum. High stakes
and stress. Shaming of schools.
• Time allotted to testing and test-prep takes away from
instruction.

What’s the solution?
• To some extent, assessment design can solve some of these
problems.
• Delayed feedback: Use of technology to expedite scoring can
greatly decrease turn-around time.
• However, it isn’t clear that large scale assessment design will solve:
• Lack of instructional utility: Results aren’t instructionally useful
due to curricular (mis)alignment, grain size of results,
• Unintended consequences: Teaching to the test, narrowing/
altering the scope and sequence of the curriculum. High stakes
and stress.

Instructional Utility
• Instructional utility has become a focus of many debates regarding
assessment and accountability.
• Two of my colleagues Carla Evans and Scott Marion wrote a book on the
topic, Understanding Instructionally Useful Assessment
• Whereas my colleagues take a more micro-view of instructional utility
(useful for day-to-day instructional decision making), I take a more macro-
view (useful for instructional decision making across some time frame).
• Clearly, large scale, annual summative assessments are not useful for day-
to-day instructional decision making.
• However, across larger time frames, those tests can be used for more
coarse grained instructional decisions.

Instructional Utility
• Do current assessment designs solve the instructional utility
problem?
• Instructional utility is NOT a property of an assessment. It’s a
function of how the assessment (if properly designed) is used.
• I would argue that current assessments are not utilized even
close to their full potential.
• I’m skeptical that new assessments will change that.
• TCAs still only occur 3 times a year — rather infrequent for
instructional decision making.

Opportunity to Learn
• Assessment designs that aren’t strictly summative (e.g., TCAs)
involve components that are more formative/benchmark.
• For example, an assessment might be administered early
in the year to see where students are in terms of
knowledge and skills (before they’ve been formally
instructed)
• How does accountability utilize student results where
opportunity to learn is questionable?

Assessment as Intervention
• Earlier I mentioned that, at their core, assessments are data
collection activities.
• Assessments, especially those claiming to be instructionally
useful, are both data collection and intervention.
• Without a THOROUGH explication of how intervention is
coupled with the assessment results, I remain skeptical that
new assessment designs will improve assessment results any
more than previous annual summative designs.
• Due to accountability systems that emphasize student
attainment, our use of data to inform student learning is stuck.

Assessment as Intervention
• As an intervention, such assessment systems should be
evaluated with regard to whether student performance
improves in comparison to other (e.g., annual, summative
assessments) systems.
• Given that new assessment systems often involve resetting
performance standards, a dubious outcome would be to see
higher student performance (e.g., % proficient) based solely
upon new (possible lower) standards being established.
Equity & Decision Making

Equity in Education: A Shared Understanding
• Definition: Equity in education means ensuring that every student
has access to the resources and opportunities they need to succeed,
recognizing and addressing disparities caused by systemic inequities.
• Key Aspects of Equity:
• Fairness: Providing what students need to achieve comparable
outcomes, rather than treating everyone identically.
• Inclusion: Ensuring all students, regardless of background or
circumstances, have meaningful access to learning.
• Responsiveness: Identifying and addressing the unique barriers
faced by different student groups.

Equity as a Guiding Principle for Decisions
• Impact of Equity on Decision-Making:
• Shapes resource allocation (e.g., funding, staffing, and materials).
• Informs the design and use of assessments to highlight disparities.
• Ensures policies and practices are inclusive and culturally relevant.
• The Stakes:
• Inequitable systems perpetuate disparities in achievement,
opportunity, and outcomes.
• Equitable decision-making can close gaps and improve success for
marginalized groups.

Challenges in Operationalizing Equity
• Common Challenges:
• Access: Digital divide or lack of resources for technology-
based assessments.
• Bias: Cultural and linguistic bias in test design or
administration.
• Opportunity to Learn: Holding students accountable for
content they haven’t had the chance to learn.
• Standardization vs. Individualization: Balancing the need for
comparability with the need for personalized approaches.

Equity-Focused Decision-Making in Action
• Practical Strategies to Promote Equity
• Data-Driven Decisions:
• Use disaggregated data to identify and address disparities.
• Focus on root causes, not just symptoms, of inequities.
• Inclusive Policies:
• Include diverse stakeholders in decision-making processes.
• Develop policies that prioritize underrepresented or underserved groups.
• Iterative Improvement:
• Regularly review assessment tools and policies for unintended
consequences.
• Adjust based on feedback and outcomes.
Policy & Practice Implications

Policy & Practice Implications: Framing the Discussion
Why Policy and Practice Matter

• Key Point: Policies shape the frameworks within which
assessments are designed, implemented, and interpreted.
Practices determine how those policies affect students and
educators.
• Objective: Explore how evolving assessments require shifts in
policy and practice to maximize their potential.

Policies Driving Assessment Innovation
Key Policy Drivers

• Federal policies like ESSA (Every Student Succeeds Act)
emphasize flexibility in assessments, including innovative
designs.
• State Initiatives: Many states are piloting competency-based
or through-course assessments to move beyond traditional
summative tests.
• Equity Mandates: Increasing attention to ensuring that
assessments are accessible and meaningful for all students.

Challenges for Policymakers
Barriers to Policy Implementation
• Scalability: Pilots of innovative assessments are difficult to
scale while maintaining quality and equity.
• Cost: Developing and implementing innovative assessments
require significant investment in technology, training, and
scoring.
• Standardization vs. Innovation: Balancing the need for
comparability across districts with the flexibility to innovate.
• Example: Challenges faced by states implementing
performance-based or through-course assessments under ESSA
waivers.

Practical Implications for Educators
Impacts on Teaching and Learning

• Instructional Alignment: Ensuring that innovative
assessments align with curriculum and teaching practices.
• Professional Development: Teachers need training to
interpret results and integrate them into instruction
effectively.
• Shifts in Practice: Moving from test-prep-centered teaching
to a more holistic approach that emphasizes deeper learning
and skill development.

The Role of Technology
Leveraging Technology for Better Outcomes

• Technology enables adaptive assessments, automated
scoring, and real-time feedback.
• Data systems must be robust to handle disaggregated
reporting and privacy concerns.
• Access equity is critical to ensure no student is left behind.

Accountability Reimagined
Rethinking Accountability Systems

• Shift focus from punitive to improvement-based
accountability.
• Use multiple measures of success, including formative and
through-course assessments.
• Incorporate growth metrics to evaluate student learning (as
opposed to student attainment).
• Use growth data to help identify what works as well as
impediments to student learning.

Policy Recommendations for the Future
Designing Policies for Evolving Assessments

• Provide funding for innovative pilot programs and scaling
successful designs.
• Require equity audits to ensure all assessments meet
accessibility and cultural relevance standards.
• Foster collaboration between policymakers, educators, and
assessment designers to create cohesive and coherent
systems.

Moving from Policy to Practice
Bridging Policy and Practice

• Establish feedback loops where policy decisions are informed
by classroom realities and vice versa.
• Invest in professional learning communities to share best
practices for assessment use.
• Pilot innovative practices in diverse contexts to identify
scalable solutions.

Conclusion & Discussion

Recap of Key Themes
Reflecting on What We’ve Explored

• The evolving landscape of educational assessments.
• What an assessment does versus what is done with the
results from the assessment.
• The critical interplay between assessment design and
accountability.
• Opportunities and challenges in policy and practice.

Lessons Learned
Key Takeaways

• Assessment Design: Innovative approaches must balance
validity, reliability, and accessibility.
• Accountability Systems: Should shift from punitive to
improvement-oriented frameworks.
• Equity: Disaggregated data and inclusive practices are
essential for addressing disparities.
• Utility: Assessments are most impactful when their results
TRULY inform (as opposed to potentially inform in some
dream scenario) beneficial, educational decisions.
